P01.note: Singular head 'face' takes 'is'; the habitual present 'whenever ... reaches' rules out the past forms. 'are prone' attracts through 'crevasses' and the plural participial opener.
P01.not_hard_because: The tense is handed over by the present 'reaches' later in the same sentence, and the singular head noun 'face' sits right before the blank.

P02.note: Plural 'tenants' plus the present 'stays' gives 'are accepting'.
P02.not_hard_because: The plural subject 'Long-term tenants' is the word directly before the blank with nothing intervening, and 'stays' hands over the present tense.

P03.note: Two independent clauses with the second explaining the overlooked detail: colon. A is a comma splice; B a run-on that garden-paths 'ignored the ring'.
P03.not_hard_because: Only one option joins two independent clauses at all (no semicolon or period offered), and D is garbled, so it reduces to spotting the comma splice.

P04.note: 'Each' is singular; 'when the sponsor replaced' needs past progressive 'was keeping'. 'were keeping' attracts through 'volunteers' and 'sites'.
P04.not_hard_because: 'Each of' is the textbook singular cue every prepared student knows, and 'replaced' hands over the past tense.

P05.note: List items contain internal commas ('a narrow-angle camera, the heaviest instrument aboard'), so items are separated by semicolons, matching the later '; and'.
P05.not_hard_because: The '; and' already printed before the last list item tells the student which mark to copy into the parallel slot.

P06.convention: Nonrestrictive participial modifier: 'those letters' is anaphoric to the single surviving bundle already named, so 'written to the copyist' can be read as added information set off by a comma.
P06.note: Intended rule is a restrictive participle after 'those' (no comma). But the passage says only one bundle survives, so 'those letters' already identifies them and A's nonrestrictive comma is defensible.
P06.not_hard_because: The demonstrative 'those' is the familiar cue for a restrictive modifier, and D (comma after 'written') is never right; but fix the exclusivity problem first.

P07.note: The harvest belongs to the seven growers who pool their fruit: plural possessive 'growers''.
P07.not_hard_because: The prior sentence opens 'Seven small apple growers ... pool their fruit', handing over both plurality and ownership before the student reaches the blank.

P08.note: The town had exactly one newspaper, so 'the Sentinel' is a nonrestrictive appositive and must be set off; the dash introduces it and runs to the end of the sentence. A (close appositive, no mark) is the strongest distractor because 'the town's newspaper the Sentinel' sounds natural.

P09.note: Plural 'copes', past event 'during the siege': 'were removed'.
P09.not_hard_because: The plural 'copes' immediately precedes the blank and 'during the siege of the city' plus 'hidden' hand over past tense; no number trap intervenes.

P10.note: Singular mass noun 'Bilingualism' with a bounded past time ('during the harbor's first expansion'): simple past 'was'. Present perfect conflicts with the closed past period.
P10.not_hard_because: The singular subject is the very first word of the sentence, and the plural attractor 'vendors' comes AFTER the blank, so it cannot mislead before the verb is chosen.

P11.convention: Colon joining two independent clauses where the second amplifies the first (Chicago 6.65); the second clause tells more about catgut, which many guides accept.
P11.note: Two independent clauses: a period works; B makes 'the tough cord...' an appositive that leaves 'also strung' without a subject; C is a run-on. D's colon is also mechanically sound between two independent clauses, so the item hinges on a semantic colon judgment the SAT does not test.
P11.not_hard_because: The comma and no-mark options fail on a visible second finite verb 'also strung', and the item's only real contest (period vs colon) is not a convention the SAT keys.

P12.note: The predicate adjective 'susceptible' is delayed past a long adverbial; 'have/has seldom ... susceptible' lacks 'been', so the perfect forms are ungrammatical. Plural 'trees' and past survey give 'were'.

P13.note: Singular 'restorer'; action interrupted by 'halted' and 'hired' (past): past progressive 'was cleaning'. 'were cleaning' attracts via 'paintings'.
P13.not_hard_because: The past verbs 'halted' and 'hired' in the same sentence hand over the tense, leaving only number, which 'the restorer' settles.

P14.note: 'pancreas' is singular despite the -s; 'unless the animals receive' sets a generic present, so 'is damaged'. 'are damaged' attracts through 'mice' and the -s ending; 'were damaged' through the following past-tense sentence.

P15.note: Introductory adverb clause 'As the crew blasted the ridge' takes a comma before the main clause. B omits it, garden-pathing 'blasted the ridge the water level'.
P15.not_hard_because: A and C produce the visibly broken 'the ridge the water level', so it is a straight two-way choice on the introductory-clause comma.

P16.convention: Semicolon joining two independent clauses: 'One photograph showed a faint gray line; the crack ... ran the full depth' is grammatical.
P16.note: The second clause explains the line, so a colon fits; but the semicolon is equally grammatical between the same two independent clauses. A is a comma splice (or misreads 'the crack...' as an appositive), B a run-on.
P16.not_hard_because: Both IC-joining marks are offered together, so the item cannot be exclusive; once fixed, the long subject 'the crack no wider ... above' is the only difficulty.

P17.note: Plural 'Field teams' takes 'have'; the wording belongs to the questionnaire, so 'its'. 'their' attracts by agreement with 'teams'.
P17.not_hard_because: The 2x2 option grid lets number and pronoun be solved independently, and the plural subject 'Field teams' opens the sentence.

P18.note: Plural 'segments', specific past occasion 'on the last night of a ... shutdown': 'were cleaned'.
P18.not_hard_because: 'on the last night of a three-week maintenance shutdown' marks a finished past event, ruling out both perfects, and 'segments' is plural right before the blank.

P19.note: Singular 'ending' (not 'verbs'); the participle 'vanished' arrives after a long adverbial, so 'has never ... vanished'; 'is never vanished' is not standard.

P20.note: Plural 'technicians' takes 'are'; the transmitters belong to the young animals (plural), so 'their'. Parallel with 'regluing'.
P20.not_hard_because: The plural subject 'technicians' sits directly before the blank, and no singular antecedent makes 'its' tempting.

P21.note: Plural 'copyists'; interrupted by 'when raiders set fire': past progressive 'were decorating'.
P21.not_hard_because: 'when raiders set fire' hands over the interrupted past progressive, and the plural subject is only three words before the blank.

P22.note: The plural verb 'record' needs a plural subject noun: 'apprentices'. Possessives leave no head noun; 'apprentice' disagrees.
P22.not_hard_because: The plural verb 'record' immediately after the blank settles the number, and the possessive options need a noun that is not there. Same template as P29.

P23.note: Plural 'parasites' takes 'are'; the agent is the wrasses (plural), so 'them'. 'it' attracts via 'grouper'.
P23.not_hard_because: The 2x2 grid splits into two independent checks, and the plural subject 'parasites' is nearly adjacent to the blank.

P24.note: Singular 'diner' takes 'judges'; the thing judged is the one precise price, matching singular 'figure', so 'it'. 'them' attracts via 'several rounded prices'.
P24.not_hard_because: The singular subject 'a diner' is right before 'typically', and the singular complement 'figure' confirms 'it' once read.

P25.note: Three lots exist, so 'gathered during an unusually dry summer' identifies which one: restrictive, no comma. B and C wrongly make it nonrestrictive.
P25.not_hard_because: 'three separate lots' in the first sentence flags the restrictive reading, the same uniqueness-count logic as P08 and P06.

P26.note: Appositive 'the widow of the shop's first foreman' is closed by the comma after 'foreman', so it opens with a comma.
P26.not_hard_because: The closing comma after 'foreman' is printed in the sentence; the student copies it.

P27.note: Singular 'curtain' takes 'was'; the neglecters are the stagehands, so 'them'.
P27.not_hard_because: The 2x2 grid splits into independent checks and the singular subject 'drop curtain' is directly before the blank.

P28.note: 'The illiterate' is an adjective used as a plural noun; 'since' requires present perfect: 'have been invisible'. 'has been' attracts via the singular look and 'a laborer's' in the prior sentence.

P29.note: Exactly one clerk; singular verb 'records' needs singular subject 'clerk'. 'clerks' records' tempts by reading 'records' as a noun.
P29.not_hard_because: 'exactly one clerk' in the previous sentence plus the singular verb 'records' right after the blank give it away. Same template as P22 and P30.

P30.note: The sketches belong to the lone geologist: singular possessive.
P30.not_hard_because: 'a lone geologist' in the first sentence and the contrast with survey teams who 'made no drawings' hand over both the number and the ownership.

P31.not_hard_because: 'on the day of the count's funeral' marks a single past event and 'bell' is singular; the plural attractor 'town' is singular too, so there is no trap.

P32.note: Plural 'engineers' takes 'have'; the reconstructed thing is the singular 'burst of telemetry', so 'it'. 'them' attracts via 'copies' and 'dishes'.
P32.not_hard_because: The 2x2 grid splits into two independent checks and the plural subject is directly before the blank.

P33.note: Plural 'plates'; simultaneous with past 'cooled': past progressive 'were being replaced'.
P33.not_hard_because: The past verb 'cooled' in the while-clause hands over the tense; plural 'plates' is the obvious head despite 'wall' and 'furnace'.

P34.note: Intransitive 'spray' ends the introductory clause; 'the vines growing ... were showing' is the main clause and needs its subject. A and B swallow 'the vines' as the object, leaving 'were showing' subjectless; D puts a semicolon after a dependent clause.

P35.note: Ellipsis: 'Whereas steel tapes do [lengthen]' with plural 'tapes' and a generic present matching 'lengthens'. 'were' tempts through 'nineteenth-century', but the elided verb is 'lengthen', not a form of 'be'.

P36.note: 'since the closure' requires present perfect; plural 'tutors' takes 'have'.
P36.not_hard_because: 'since' hands over the present perfect, the same tense cue as P37 and P38.

P37.note: 'since the housing-market crash' requires present perfect; singular 'study' takes 'has'. 'have been' attracts via 'interns'.
P37.not_hard_because: 'since' hands over the tense exactly as in P36 and P38, leaving only the 'study of interns' attractor.

P38.note: 'since the network rewrote' requires present perfect; singular 'ointment' takes 'has'.
P38.not_hard_because: 'since' hands over the tense, the third use of the same cue in this render (P36, P37), and 'ointment' is singular right before the blank.

P39.note: Singular 'receiver' takes 'is'; the tracked objects are the meteoroids (plural), so 'them'. 'are' attracts via 'domes'.
P39.not_hard_because: The 2x2 grid splits into independent checks, and the singular head 'receiver' is easy to find despite 'twin domes'.

P40.note: Singular 'editor' takes 'was'; the revised object is the novel (its closing scene), so 'it'. 'them' attracts via 'sonnets', the nearest plural noun.
P40.not_hard_because: The 2x2 grid splits into two checks and 'cutting ... from its closing scene' after the blank confirms the singular antecedent.

tells: In every punctuation item where an option puts the mark after the SECOND word ('ignored the,' P03, 'letters written,' P06, 'newspaper the,' P08, 'lot gathered,' P25), that option loses; the one exception is P15 ('blasted the ridge,'), so the shape is strikable in four of five appearances.

An explicit 'since' makes the present-perfect option the key in P28, P36, P37 and P38. Without 'since', the perfect option loses in P10, P12, P13, P18 and P21. P19 is the only exception (its key is 'has never', with no 'since'). So the tense can almost always be read from one word.
Possessive/number items all hand over the count in the prior sentence ('Seven ... growers' P07, 'exactly one clerk' P29, 'a lone geologist' P30, 'several youths' P22).

Pronoun 2x2 items (P17, P20, P23, P24, P27, P32, P39, P40) each decompose into two independent binary checks; the pronoun distractor is always the nearest noun of the wrong number (sonnets P40, copies P32, domes P39, grouper P23).
Two items offer two IC-joining marks at once (P11 period vs colon, P16 colon vs semicolon), so neither can be exclusive.
near_duplicates: noun count given in prior sentence decides possessive or plural form
uniqueness count decides restrictive vs nonrestrictive modifier
verb number crossed with pronoun number in a 2x2 grid
plain subject-verb number with a past-time clause handing over tense
two independent clauses joined by colon, period or semicolon
delayed participle or adjective after an adverbial makes the auxiliary choice
